name: Karata
confidence_why: Magomedbekova's 1971 grammar, the Magomedova and Khalidova 2001 dictionary (stress marked on every headword, minimal pairs on p. 444), Pakhrudinova 2004, Gadzhieva 2007 for Tukita and Dalgatov 2015 and 2017 for Siwukh all describe Karata stress as weak, dynamic and mobile with an occasional contrastive function, whereas Pasquereau 2025, the most recent fieldworker, has not perceived a consistent stress pattern and leaves the existence of a stress system open, so the type of system is genuinely questioned but the weight of first-hand description favours weak mobile stress.
catalog_citation: Далгатов, И. Х. 2015. Фонетические особенности сивухского диалекта каратинского языка. Актуальные проблемы гуманитарных и естественных наук, № 5-1 (3 pp; CyberLeninka, open).
catalog_locator: p. 2 (CyberLeninka offprint, no printed pagination), stress paragraphs of the article
catalog_quote: Ударение в сивухском диалекте также слабое динамическое, подвижное. ... Чаще всего в двухсложных словах с открытым типом слога в конце ударение падает на первый от начала слог, а в двухсложных словах с конечным закрытым типом - на второй слог. На второй слог ударение также падает в двухсложных существительных в формах множественного числа и косвенных основ. В трех-четырех- и пятисложных словах ударение разноместное.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Both the existing grammar (Magomedbekova 1971) and the dictionary (Magomedova and Khalidova 2001) describe Karata as having lexical, contrastive stress. Minimal pairs illustrating this are provided in Magomedova and Khalidova (2001: 444), for instance: ˈhadir ‘to the face’ vs. haˈdir ‘to here’, and ˈhaň’:u ‘week’ vs. haˈň’:u ‘comb’. However, based on my research so far, it is not clear that Karata indeed has such a system. Several factors suggest that stress may not be a salient or contrastive feature of the language. First, I, along with colleagues, have not perceived a consistent stress pattern in Karata.
new_statements.citation: Pasquereau, Jérémy. Accepted (author manuscript dated 10 March 2025). "Karata (Nakh-Daghestanian)". In: The Caucasian Languages. An International Handbook, vol. 2 (HSK). Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. §2.4 Prosody, p. 7.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata: 59 pp., pdfTeX, created 2025-03-10; title page "Karata / Jérémy Pasquereau / March 10, 2025"). Section 2.4 Prosody is on PDF page 7 = printed page 7, and the quoted passage from "Both the existing grammar (Magomedbekova 1971) and the dictionary.." through ".. have not perceived a consistent stress pattern in Karata." is there word for word; the text shows the stress marks as straight double quotes but the rendered page (page render) prints them as the TIPA primary-stress mark ˈ, so the compiler ˈhadir / haˈdir, ˈhaň’:u / haˈň’:u is faithful to the printed page. The rest of the section says the reported minimal pairs and discussions with the dictionary's second au…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Russian descriptive tradition (Magomedbekova 1971; Magomedova & Khalidova 2001, which marks stress on every headword; Pakhrudinova 2004 metatony pairs; Dalgatov 2015/2017 and Gadzhieva 2007 for the Siwukh and Tukita varieties) treats Karata stress as weak, dynamic, mobile and lexically/grammatically contrastive: in disyllables it tends to fall on the first syllable when the final syllable is open and on the second when it is closed or in plural/oblique forms; in longer words it is 'разноместное' (free); stress shift from first to second syllable derives nouns from verbal nouns. The most recent first-hand description (Pasquereau) reports that he and colleagues cannot perceive a consistent stress pattern, that the reported minimal pairs did not verify, that Karata may have a Bagvalal-like three-way split (clear stress / weak stress / no apparent stress), and he leaves stress unmarked with the question open. Net: sources disagree; no fixed-position rule is stated for Karata proper.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Pasquereau: reported minimal pairs (dictionary p. 444) not confirmed in his data; possible three-way word split as in Bagvalal (Kibrik 2001). Gadzhieva 2007 (Tukita): infinitives stressed on the infinitive suffix -еду; plural and oblique-stem forms of disyllabic nouns take second-syllable stress. Dalgatov 2014/2017 (Siwukh): stress distinguishes 'came' vs 'made come' and singular vs plural.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Pasquereau's statement concerns the variety of Karata village (isolated words, minimal pairs, recorded texts); Dalgatov and Gadzhieva describe the Siwukh subdialect and the Tukita dialect respectively (citation-form words, noun paradigms).
new_statements.identity_note: Pasquereau's sketch describes the variety of Karata village (Glottolog dialect kara1516 'Karata dialect'); he treats Tukita as a separate language, not covered. The Dalgatov statements concern the Siwukh (Сивух) subdialect of Karata proper and the Gadzhieva statement the Tukita dialect (no separate Glottolog code under kara1474 in 5.1's children list).

tone_statements.citation: Nikolayev, Sergei L. & Sergei A. Starostin. 1994. A North Caucasian Etymological Dictionary. Edited by S. A. Starostin. Moscow: Asterisk Publishers. Introduction: 'Sources' p. 10 (no. 12 Karata) and §1.4 'From PA to modern Andian languages', §1.4.4 'Root structure and prosody', p. 109 (pagination of the authors' re-typeset PDF of the introduction).
tone_statements.quote: Judging by the results of the MSU expeditions of 1973 — 1978, all modern Andian languages possess systems of tonal (melodic, sometimes mixed dynamic-melodic) accentuation with significant pitch distinctions. However, a careful description and a corpus of accented lexical material are unfortunately still lacking. Therefore, despite some observations already made (see [Starostin 1978]), it is yet early to talk about the PA accent reconstruction.
tone_statements.locator: Introduction, section 1.4 'From PA to modern Andian languages', 1.4.4 'Root structure and prosody', last paragraph, p. 109 (whose table of contents starts the Dictionary at p. 200); Karata source note: 'Sources', item 12 'Karata', p. 10; transcription note on unmarked tonal distinctions p. 15.

sources.locator: Introduction, section 1.4 'From PA to modern Andian languages', 1.4.4 'Root structure and prosody', last paragraph, p. 109 (whose table of contents starts the Dictionary at p. 200); Karata source note: 'Sources', item 12 'Karata', p. 10; transcription note on unmarked tonal distinctions p. 15.
sources.note: Asserts that all modern Andian languages (a group that in this work explicitly includes Karata and its Tokita dialect) have 'tonal (melodic, sometimes mixed dynamic-melodic) accentuation with significant pitch distinctions', while stating that careful descriptions and accented corpora are lacking and referring to Starostin 1978 for preliminary Avar-Andian tonal correspondences; Karata forms in the dictionary carry only Magomedbekova's dynamic-stress marks, tonal distinctions being left unmarked. This is the Moscow-school claim behind the 'uncertain' prosodic status of Karata; it is not a Kara…
